The first Saturday in April, 7:30 in the morning, at Mrs Fumiko’s teahouse in Kyoto, next to the temple. Today the teahouse turns 50. Until 10, when the guests arrive, everyone helps. Rosa Elena (1 year, 2 and a half months) toddles unsteadily between the tables.
Good morning, everyone. Thank you for helping me today; you’re a great help to me.
Not at all. Tell us anything you need. The tables are already set out.
Mihai, you’re up early! Did you manage to sleep well last night?
Actually, I was nervous and couldn’t really sleep. And yesterday I even spilled the tea in front of Mrs Fumiko…
(Laughing) Please don’t worry. With tea and with languages alike, the more you make mistakes, the better you get.
Mrs Fumiko, may I take lots of photos today?
Of course. We’ll ask you to be our photographer for the whole day today.
Yay! And I’ll take the photo for Grandpa too, okay?
That’s right, the photo of the spoon. Grandpa wants to see with his own eyes whether the spoon was really used.
(Opening a wooden box) Here it is. I’ve kept it carefully put away. I intend to use it today for the first time.
Oh, how beautiful! The cherry wood still looks new.
I had decided that the first cup would be for Hana-chan. Mihai, would that be all right?
As a doctor… if it’s just one sip. A lukewarm, weak hōjicha shouldn’t do her any harm.
Mihai, you’re wearing your doctor face again.
(Laughing) By the way, Mihai, you passed N4, didn’t you? Congratulations!
Thank you. I thought I might fail the listening, but somehow…
Well done! With the baby crying at night, and still you worked so hard.
Because Hana-chan slept nicely for him!
Yes. I’ve already bought the N3 book. This time I’ll put it up high so Hana-chan can’t chew it.
(Looking at the clock) Oh, it’s already eight! I have to change Hana-chan before the guests arrive.
Look, Hana-chan is staring at the box with the spoon.
(Laughing) It seems Hana-chan can’t wait to drink either. Well then, everyone, thank you in advance for your help today.

kin-chō: ん before ち sounds like a normal “n”, and the “o” in ちょう is long (cho-o). cho-o-ka-i: a long “o” again. Don’t say a short “kincho”: ちょ is one short syllable, then you stretch the vowel.
shi-n-ka-n-se-n: six equal beats, even though an English ear hears only three syllables! Each ん is a full beat. Before か, ん sounds like the “ng” in “sing”; at the end, it’s lightly nasal.

yu-no-mi: three equal syllables. i-p-pa-i: っ is a short stop before “pa”, as in “ip-pai”. hi-to-ku-chi: the “i” in “hi” and the “u” in “ku” are barely heard (between voiceless consonants): “h’tok’chi”.
1. N4 verb forms in a single table (ch. 21, 22, 24, 30–34)

The whole N4 level has given the verb one new “outfit” after another. Here they all are, for a group 1 verb (いく, to go), a group 2 verb (たべる, to eat) and the two irregular ones (する, くる). If you can say the rows of the table with your eyes closed, you’ve mastered the skeleton of N4 grammar.

All the examples from today’s dialogue: ねられません (potential, “I couldn’t sleep”), まちがえれば (～ば), つかわれた (direct passive), あかちゃん に なかれながら (suffering passive + ながら), かじられない (passive), きがえさせなきゃ (causative: “make her change” = change her clothes).

The big trap: たべられる (gr. 2) can be POTENTIAL (“can eat”), PASSIVE (“is eaten”) and RESPECT (“eats”, ch. 36). Context decides. In everyday speech the potential is often shortened: たべれる, ねれる (ら-ぬき) — you’ll hear it, but in the exam write the full form.

Memory trick for group 1: the potential moves to the “e” row (いけ-る), ～ば also to “e” (いけ-ば), the volitional to “o” (いこ-う), the passive and causative to “a” (いか-れる, いか-せる). So: a = others do something (passive / causative), e = can / if, o = let’s.
Japanese keeps track: who does the favour and for whom. The same “help” is said differently depending on the direction.
はなちゃん が ねて あげた (Hana-chan “did him the favour” of sleeping)
ケンジさん が おくって くれた (Kenji took me to the airport)
しゃしんや さん に なって もらいましょう (we’ll ask you to be the photographer)
てつだって いただいて (that you are helping me)
つくって くださった (Grandpa kindly made it)
Respect (尊敬語) — about the other person
お + stem + に なる (おつき に なる)
お + stem + する (おもち します)
お + stem + ください (おめしあがり ください)
Keigo of respect is NEVER put on your own actions: ✗ わたし が めしあがります → ✓ いただきます. And remember うち と そと (ch. 37): speaking to a customer about your boss, you use humble language (イオネスク は もうして おります).
English mostly gets by with “if”; Japanese has six tools. Choose according to what you want to say:
“if it’s a matter of…”, a reaction to what was said
After ～と and ～ば you don’t usually put a request or a wish (✗ きょうと に つく と、でんわ して ください). Use ～たら: ✓ きょうと に ついたら、でんわ して ください.
Quick test: can I say “whether” instead of “if”? → か どうか. Can I say “after”? → たら. Is it a law of nature? → と. Am I reacting to what someone else said? → なら.
From “I’m convinced” to “maybe”, plus “it looks” and “I heard”. They all go at the end of the sentence:
Don’t mix up the two そう: あたらしそう (stem + そう = “looks new”) and あたらしい そう です (full form + そう = “I heard it’s new”). And はず rests on facts, not on wishes: ✗ ごうかく する はず (because I want it).

Watch out for transitive / intransitive pairs (ch. 28): あける / あく, しめる / しまる, つける / つく, ならべる / ならぶ. ～て ある takes the transitive verb (someone put them there): ならべて ある. ～て いる usually takes the intransitive one: ならんで いる (they stand in a row).
しまう has two lives: as an independent verb it means “to put away” (スプーン を しまう); after ～て it means “completely / unfortunately” (こぼして しまう). The dialogue has both: しまって おきました and こぼして しまった.
～つもり / volitional + と おもう
stem + やすい / にくい
A request doesn’t follow のに (✗ さむい のに、きて ください). And ために needs the same subject and a verb of will; for “so as not to” or verbs without will, you use ように: かじられない ように おく (you’ll meet it often at N3).

Did you notice that today’s dialogue mixes them all? That’s real Japanese: no form lives on its own. Reread the dialogue and count: how many forms from the tables in explanations 1–6 can you find? (Answer: more than 15.)
7. What comes next: the N3 level

Congratulations! With this chapter you’ve finished N4, just like Mihai. Now you can understand everyday conversations if people speak a little slowly, and you can read simple texts about ordinary things. N3 is the “bridge” between basic Japanese (N5–N4) and intermediate-advanced Japanese (N2–N1).

ふみこさん の あいさつ — Mrs Fumiko’s speech
At noon, before the tea, Mrs Fumiko speaks to the guests. Listen for how much keigo (ch. 36–40) and how many N4 forms you recognise.
Dear guests, thank you for coming today, busy as you are.
I opened this teahouse fifty years ago, one spring, when I was still young.
At the beginning there were days when not a single customer came.
If I was still able to carry on, it is because you supported me.
This year my sister came from Madrid, and dear friends from Hiroshima and from Romania.
Showing my sister this teahouse was my dream for a long time.
I believe tea is something that grows deeper the more you make it.
And from now on, as long as I am healthy, I intend to keep the teahouse going.
Please enjoy it at your leisure.

ごじゅうねん の ゆのみ — The fifty-year-old teacup
One Wednesday in early April, Mihai, Ana and Rosa Elena arrived at Kansai airport. From Bucharest, with one change of plane, the journey had taken sixteen hours in all.
Because Rosa Elena drank milk during take-off and landing, she didn’t cry even once. “See? If you do as the doctor says, everything’s fine,” said Mihai, terribly pleased with himself.
Mrs Suzuki was waiting for them in the arrivals hall with a small suitcase. She had flown alone from Madrid.
“Kenji took me to the airport. And he’s looking after Tama for me again.”
When she saw Rosa Elena toddling, Mrs Suzuki’s eyes went wide: “Oh my! She can walk already!”
On the train, Mrs Suzuki sat Rosa Elena on her lap and told her about Tama in Madrid.
Rosa Elena had taken her first steps right on her birthday, when she turned one. She had faithfully kept her promise to her grandpa in the village.

Through the train window, cherry blossoms began to appear. From Kyoto station they took a taxi, and when they got out in a narrow lane near the temple, Mrs Fumiko was standing in front of the teahouse.
“Welcome, Hana-chan. At last we meet.” When Mrs Fumiko bowed deeply, Rosa Elena copied her and bobbed her little head too.
In front of the white curtain at the entrance, Mrs Suzuki suddenly stopped. “So this is… Fumiko’s teahouse. The one I couldn’t come to even once in fifty years.”
Without a word, Mrs Fumiko took her sister by the hand and led her inside. Stroking the old wooden pillar, Mrs Suzuki said, “You looked after it on your own, all these years.”
Mrs Fumiko took a white teacup down from the shelf. A cup no one had ever drunk from.
“I bought it when I opened the teahouse. I thought that if you came one day, you could drink from it.”
That day, the cup that had waited fifty years was finally used. Ana quietly squeezed Mihai’s hand.
That evening Ana also passed on the greetings from the old ladies in the village. Mrs Fumiko was delighted: “I still remember the taste of that cozonac.”
The next day at noon, Haruka and Sakura came from Hiroshima by shinkansen. Sakura, who had turned ten, had grown a lot. Around her neck hung her ever-present camera.
“Hana-chan!” Sakura flung down her bag and knelt on the floor. Rosa Elena stared at the unknown girl and hid behind Mihai’s legs.
“…So she’s scared of me after all?” Sakura said sadly. Then Haruka began to sing softly: “Nennen korori yo, okorori yo…”
It was the song Daddy sings to her every night. Rosa Elena peeked out and toddled towards Sakura. Then she grabbed the camera strap tightly.
“She caught me!” Sakura was crying and laughing at the same time. “At last we meet, my flower little sister.” Haruka quietly took a photo of the two of them.
From that day on, wherever she went, Rosa Elena started toddling after Sakura.
On Friday they all went to the temple’s moss garden. It was the very temple where Mrs Fumiko had got the amulet. Petal by petal, cherry blossoms were falling onto the green moss.
Mrs Fumiko carried Rosa Elena in her arms and walked slowly along the narrow path between the moss.
“The more you look, the more beautiful it is,” said Mrs Suzuki, and Mrs Fumiko laughed: “Sister, you said that in Bucharest too.”
Rosa Elena wanted to touch the moss and kept reaching out. But they say moss is very fragile, so you mustn’t touch it. When Ana said “No!”, Rosa Elena pouted.
“It seems she already understands Mummy’s words,” laughed Mihai. Sakura took so many photos that her camera battery ran out.
Saturday, the day of the anniversary, was clear from the morning. Mrs Fumiko and Mrs Suzuki, in matching cherry-pink kimonos, welcomed their guests.
An old lady who had been coming there for fifty years, the monk from the temple next door, Yuki, who had rushed over from Tokyo. The teahouse filled up with people.
Ana handed over the present from the pupils at the school in Bucharest where she had started teaching again in September: a drawing by Andrei of cherry trees and the teahouse.

In the afternoon, Mrs Fumiko opened a little wooden box in front of everyone. “This is the spoon that a grandfather from a village in Romania kindly carved from the cherry tree in his yard. Allow me to use it today for the first time.”
Mrs Fumiko scooped up hōjicha leaves with the spoon and made a lukewarm, weak tea. When Mihai sat Rosa Elena on his lap, Sakura raised her camera: “I’m taking the photo for Grandpa!”
Rosa Elena took a sip and pulled a face. Everyone laughed. But straight away she reached for the cup again.
“See? The more you drink, the better it tastes,” said Mrs Fumiko, her eyes crinkling in a smile. Click. Sakura’s camera caught the moment.
Mrs Suzuki was dabbing her eyes with a handkerchief. “I wish I could have shown Mother too.” “Sister, I’m sure she’s watching from somewhere.”
That same day a photo arrived from Kenji in Madrid: Tama asleep next to a bowl of ramen. It said: “Tama’s celebrating too.”
That evening Mihai sent the photo to Elena. The next day Elena went to the village and showed it to Grandpa.
At the other end of the line, Grandpa was silent for a long time. “…I see. So our cherry tree made it to Kyoto too.”
Then he said, smiling a little: “Next time it’s the little one’s turn to make me a tea.”
After hanging up, Mihai sat down on the veranda. In the garden, the cherry trees glowed white in the night.
A year ago, Rosa Elena had only just been born, and Mihai would open his workbook rubbing his sleepy eyes. Now his N4 certificate was in his bag. But on his lap was already the N3 book.
Ana came with two cups of tea and sat down next to him. “What are you thinking about?” “That our Japanese has only just begun.”
“Then the longer we keep at it, the more fun it’ll be.”
Tomorrow they plan to go to Miyajima together. It’s Sakura’s turn to keep her promise to show Hana-chan the torii gate.
From behind the sliding doors came the laughter of Mrs Suzuki and Mrs Fumiko. Fifty years’ worth of stories showed no sign of ending.
In the room next door, Rosa Elena was sleeping peacefully, still holding tight to Sakura’s camera strap.
And so Mihai and Ana’s N4 year came to an end. And once again, a new year begins.
